title: Could Africa Become Russia's Oil Lifeline as U.S. Tariffs Threaten India and China?
excerpt: President Trump's new sanctions law authorizes 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil. With India and China in the frame, Moscow may look to Africa — but the economics of that pivot are far from simple.
body:
• President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on September 18, authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian crude or gas.
  • India and China — the top two buyers, at about 1.6 million and 1.1 million barrels a day of Russian crude in August, per S&P Global — face the greatest exposure, though the tariffs are discretionary, not automatic.
  • With its two biggest customers under threat, Moscow may deepen energy ties with Africa, where Putin has pointed to more than 30 Russian energy projects and sharply rising fuel exports.
  • India says it remains "firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people," while industry groups are urging New Delhi to engage Washington to protect exporters.

If India and China can no longer buy Russian oil without facing punishing American tariffs, where does Moscow's crude go? That is the question hanging over global energy markets after President Donald Trump signed sweeping Russia sanctions legislation on September 18 — and a Mint analysis asks whether Africa could become Vladimir Putin's next energy network.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 gives the U.S. president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. India and China, the two biggest buyers of seaborne Russian crude, sit squarely in the frame — but the tariffs are not automatic. The White House must first identify which countries qualify, set rates and covered products.

Context & Background

The bill cleared the House 262-159 on September 16 and the Senate 86-11 in August — the first major Ukraine-related legislation to pass Congress in more than two years. Beyond the tariff authority, it sanctions Russian officials, senior figures and oligarchs, banks and financial institutions, the energy and defense sectors, and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to move Russian oil around Western sanctions. It also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

Supporters say the aim is to starve the Kremlin of the revenue sustaining its war in Ukraine and push Putin toward negotiations. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who lobbied lawmakers ahead of the vote, called the legislation "an extremely powerful tool." House Speaker Mike Johnson said it put "maximum pressure" on Russia's war machine. Not all Democrats agreed: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries warned the tariff powers would raise costs for American families and called the sanctions provisions full of "loopholes."

"An extremely powerful tool."

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine

The signing came about a week before Trump is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.

Impact & Analysis

The Africa pivot is not starting from zero. At the 2023 BRICS summit in Johannesburg, Putin told African leaders that Russia would remain a "reliable partner" for food and fuel, said Russia had more than 30 energy projects across African countries, and claimed exports of Russian crude, petroleum products and liquefied natural gas to Africa had grown 2.6 times in two years. The expanded BRICS — now including Egypt and Ethiopia — gives Moscow a ready-made diplomatic framework for deeper ties.

But replacing Asia's volumes is a different order of magnitude. India imported about 1.6 million barrels a day of Russian crude in August and China about 1.1 million, according to S&P Global data reported by the Energy Tribune. Redirecting anything close to that toward Africa would test the continent's demand, refinery capacity, ports and financing — with a built-in catch: African buyers that ramped up Russian crude purchases could themselves land in the law's top-five crosshairs.

Whether the pivot materializes will depend on Moscow's discounts, the shipping routes it can secure outside Western insurance and finance, and — above all — whether Washington treats the tariff threat as a lever for concessions or a weapon to fire.

Diaspora Angle

India is among the most exposed: it imported about 1.6 million barrels a day of Russian crude in August, and the government has said it remains "firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people." The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry has urged New Delhi to engage Washington to protect exporters, according to ANI reporting carried by Mint. For the diaspora, the stakes run from fuel prices back home to the U.S.-India trade ties many Indian-American businesses depend on.

What's Next

Everything now hinges on implementation: the White House and the USTR must identify qualifying countries, set tariff rates and covered products, with reviews every 180 days and waivers for national security. India has said it is monitoring the law and will protect its trade and energy security while diplomatic consultations begin. Whether the tariffs become a lever or a weapon will shape oil flows well beyond Russia.
